# Introduction

Computational tools are now at the heart of modern palaeontology. From cleaning datasets to running complex analyses, software underpins much of what we do. This module introduces you to [*palaeoverse*](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org), an R package to help you get your palaeontological data into the right shape for analyses and keep your code clear.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Install and load *palaeoverse*, as well as locate its documentation, vignettes, and help resources
- Understand the design and potential applications of *palaeoverse*
- Apply *palaeoverse* functions to explore, prepare, and visualise fossil occurrence data
- Identify the functions available in *palaeoverse* and implement them into your own research

## Pre-requisites and related modules

You should be comfortable with basic R (data frames, functions, installing packages). Experience with fossil occurrence data, for example from the [Paleobiology Database (PBDB)](https://paleobiodb.org/#/), is also helpful but not required.

If needed, you can refer to our [R Basics]() module. **LINK NEEDS ADDING**

## Why use *palaeoverse*

Palaeobiological analyses rarely go straight from raw data to results. You will likely start by carrying out routine tasks such as check taxonomic names, binning occurrences into time bins, reconstructing the palaeogeographic distribution of your occurrence dataset, and much more. These steps are essential but repetitive, and often rewritten for every project. *palaeoverse* aims to make these efforts more reusable, reproducible, and readable by:

1. Replacing long, bespoke scripts with a few clear lines of code
2. Using consistent function names, arguments, and outputs to make your scripts easier to read and share
3. Developing well-documented, tested, and peer-reviewed functions which are transparent and robust

# Design principles

*palaeoverse* is built around a small set of principles that shape how the functions look and behave.

1. Built around occurrence data: most functions expect an occurrence `data.frame` as input

::: {.callout-note}
## Anatomy of an occurrence dataset

Each row is a single record of something present at a particular place and time. That "something" is usually a taxon, but it does not have to be. For example, in the in-built `reefs` dataset, each row is a fossil reef rather than a species.

Occurrence data typically include columns describing:

- *Taxonomy* (e.g. accepted name, genus, and family)
- *Age* (e.g. maximum and minimum ages or named intervals)
- *Location* (e.g. longitude and latitude)
- *Additional context* (formation, collection, or reference)
:::

2. Modular: each function does one job well, you can use a single function in isolation or chain several together

```{r}
#| label: isolation-chain
#| eval: false

# Load library
library(palaeoverse)
# Get example data
data(tetrapods)
# Get time bins
bins <- time_bins(interval = "Phanerozoic", rank = "stage")
# Bin data temporally
tetrapods |>
  bin_time(bins = bins, method = "mid")
```

3. Flexible: functions are not tied to a single data source (e.g. Paleobiology Database), column names are generally arguments rather than fixed requirements, so you can use data from any source with ease

```{r}
#| label: flexible
#| eval: false

# Load library
library(palaeoverse)
# Example data
data(tetrapods)
# Use custom input `name`
tax_range_time(occdf = tetrapods, name = "accepted_name")
```

4. Transparent and reproducible: all code is documented and open source, so it can be reviewed by anyone
5. Well documented: every function has a help page with worked examples to help users get started
6. Community driven: developed openly, with peer-review from fellow researchers, and users encouraged to suggest features, report bugs, and contribute

# Applications

Typical applications for *palaeoverse* include:

- Cleaning and standardising occurrence data (e.g. checking taxonomic names and removing duplicates)
- Binning occurrences into temporal and spatial units (e.g. for analyses of diversity and biogeography)
- Estimating the position of organisms at time of deposition (i.e. palaeogeographic reconstruction)
- Summarising taxa, such as estimating temporal and geographic ranges

These steps can feed into a wide range of downstream analyses, including diversity dynamics, macroevolution, macroecology and biogeography.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where does palaeoverse fit?

Think of palaeoverse as the bridge between raw occurrence data and the analytical methods you want to apply.
:::

# Installation

To install the current release of [*palaeoverse*](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org) from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/palaeoverse/index.html) (recommended), use:

```{r}
#| label: install-palaeoverse
#| eval: false

install.packages("palaeoverse")
```

To install the development version, first install the [remotes](https://remotes.r-lib.org/) package, and then use `install_github()` to install [palaeoverse](https://github.com/palaeoverse/palaeoverse/) directly from GitHub:

```{r}
#| label: install-remotes
#| eval: false

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("palaeoverse/palaeoverse")
```

Now you are able to load palaeoverse:

```{r}
#| label: load-palaeoverse

library(palaeoverse)
```

# Getting help

Everyone gets stuck with using new tools, and knowing where to look is one of the most useful skills you can develop. As with most packages, *palaeoverse* has several layers of support, from built-in documentation to wider community support.

The *palaeoverse* [website](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org) hosts the full function documentation, vignettes and news on new releases. It is searchable and can be easier to browse than the help pages in R for some users.

![You can see all available functions and their documentation via the package's dedicated website [reference guide](https://palaeoverse.palaeoverse.org/reference/index.html).](img/palaeoverse-reference.png)

If you are familiar with GitHub, you can also check existing issues within the dedicated [repository](https://github.com/palaeoverse/palaeoverse/), as someone may already have asked your question. If you cannot find an answer to your question, you can open an [issue](https://github.com/palaeoverse/palaeoverse/issues) on GitHub (see [best practises](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/articles/reprex-dos-and-donts.html)).

GitHub can be a *scary* place if you are not familiar with it. So, you can also reach out by [email](mailto:info@palaeoverse.org) if you are facing difficulties or join our [Zulip](https://palaeoverse.org/zulip/join-zulip/), and raise a topic.

::: {.callout-note}
## Citing palaeoverse

A quick note on behalf of the developers. If you use *palaeoverse* in your research, please cite the [associated publication](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14099). Citations are one of the main ways our work is acknowledged, and they help keep the package maintained and improved ([read more on this topic](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-023-02008-w)). You can access the appropriate citation via:

```{r}
#| label: cite-palaeoverse
#| eval: false

citation("palaeoverse")
```
:::
